orig_9709_m1_energy_work_done.description: Calculate signed work, identify zero work and use the correct displacement for a resistance or for weight.

sections.title: Which force component does work?
sections.label: Resolve along the displacement
sections.intro: Work describes the energy transferred by a force as its point of application moves. For a constant force and a straight displacement, resolve the force along the movement before multiplying by the distance.

blocks.html: If the angle between force and displacement is \(\theta\), use \(W=Fd\cos\theta\). One joule is one newton metre.

figure.alt: An angled pulling force F and a horizontal displacement d start at the same point. The angle between them is marked theta.
figure.caption: The work uses the component of \(F\) along the displacement arrow. Here the indicated angle is the one used in \(Fd\cos\theta\).

blocks.html: The angle must be measured from the actual displacement direction. An angle to a wall or a vertical axis may need to be converted.

blocks.title: Find signed work from an angle
blocks.prompt: The sample carriage moves \(9\,\mathrm m\) in a straight line. A constant force has magnitude \(36\,\mathrm N\) at angle \(30^\circ\) to the displacement. Find the signed work done by that force.
blocks.hint: Find the angle between the force and the displacement, then use cosine with its sign.
blocks.solution:
The force component along the displacement is \(F\cos\theta=18 \sqrt{3}\) newtons.

Multiply the signed component by the distance. \(W=36\times 9\times\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)=162 \sqrt{3}\).

The force does \(162 \sqrt{3}\,\mathrm J\) of work. This is positive because the force partly helps the motion.

sections.title: When does a force do negative work?
sections.label: Read the work sign
sections.intro: When the force has a component back against the displacement, that component does negative work. This can occur even when another force keeps the body moving forwards.

blocks.html: Acute \(\theta\) gives positive work, a right angle gives zero, and obtuse \(\theta\) gives negative work.
Changing a work result to a positive number loses information about how the force transfers energy.

blocks.title: Find signed work from an angle
blocks.prompt: The sample carriage moves \(8\,\mathrm m\) in a straight line. A constant force has magnitude \(30\,\mathrm N\) at angle \(\theta\) to the displacement. The cosine of this angle is \(- \frac{4}{5}\). Find the signed work done by that force.

retry.feedback: The force has an opposing component because the cosine is negative. Retain the negative sign.

blocks.hint: Find the angle between the force and the displacement, then use cosine with its sign.
blocks.solution:
The force component along the displacement is \(F\cos\theta=-24\) newtons.

Multiply the signed component by the distance. \(W=30\times 8\times\left(- \frac{4}{5}\right)=-192\).

The force does \(-192\,\mathrm J\) of work. This is negative because the force has a component opposing motion.

sections.title: Can a force act and still do no work?
sections.label: Identify zero work
sections.intro: A force does zero work if its point of application stays still, or if it acts perpendicular to the displacement. A normal force on a fixed smooth track is an important example.

blocks.html: For \(\theta=90^\circ\), \(\cos\theta=0\). For zero displacement, the work is zero regardless of the angle.
A large normal reaction does not transfer energy to a particle sliding along a fixed supporting surface.

blocks.title: Recognise zero work without displacement
blocks.prompt: The load remains stationary throughout an interval while a constant force of \(75\,\mathrm N\) acts on it. Find the signed work done by that force.
blocks.hint: Mechanical work requires displacement of the point where the force acts.
blocks.solution:
The point of application is stationary, so there is no displacement to use in the work calculation.

The force does \(0\,\mathrm J\) of work.

sections.title: What does work done against resistance mean?
sections.label: Separate work and loss
sections.intro: A resistance pointing back along the path does negative work. The phrase ‘work done against resistance’ asks for the corresponding positive amount of energy dissipated.

blocks.html: For constant resisting force magnitude \(R\) and length \(d\), its signed work is \(-Rd\), and the positive loss is \(Rd\).
Use the distance travelled while the resistance acts. A vertical rise or a horizontal projection does not give the resistive work on a slope.

blocks.title: Distinguish work by and against a resistance
blocks.prompt: A transport sled moves \(35\,\mathrm m\) against a constant resistance of \(16\,\mathrm N\). Find the signed work done by resistance and the energy lost to resistance.

fields.label: Work done by resistance in joules

blocks.hint: Work done by resistance is negative. The amount of work done against it is positive.
blocks.solution:
The force points opposite to the displacement, so its own work is \(-Rd\).

The product of the two magnitudes is \(560\,\mathrm J\).

Resistance does \(-560\,\mathrm J\) of work. The amount of energy transferred away from mechanical energy is \(560\,\mathrm J\).

sections.title: Why does gravity use vertical displacement?
sections.label: Find the work by gravity
sections.intro: Weight points downwards. Its work depends on the signed vertical displacement \(\Delta h\), even when the route is longer than that displacement.

blocks.html: \(W_g=-mg\Delta h\), with upwards positive. On a straight incline of length \(d\), the height gain uphill is \(d\sin\alpha\).

figure.alt: A sloped path from A to B shows an uphill arrow and a dashed vertical height marker to the right.
figure.caption: Use the vertical height change \(h\) for work by weight. The path length \(d\) is used for a force resisting motion along the ramp.

blocks.html: For a downhill motion \(\Delta h<0\). Gravity then does positive work.
Draw the vertical height difference separately from the length of the route.

blocks.title: Calculate work by weight on a slope
blocks.prompt: A particle, modelled as a instrument sled, has mass \(8\,\mathrm{kg}\) moves \(13\,\mathrm m\) down a slope. The sine of the inclination is \(\frac{5}{13}\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Give its signed height change (upwards positive) and the work done by gravity.

retry.feedback: The particle goes downhill. Take the provided upwards-positive sign convention into account.

blocks.hint: Use the signed vertical change, not the distance measured along the plane, when multiplying by weight.
blocks.solution:
Only vertical displacement enters the work done by the vertical weight. The vertical change is \(-5\,\mathrm m\).

Gravity acts downwards, so signed work is \(W_g=-mg\,\Delta h=400\) joules.

The height change is \(-5\,\mathrm m\) and work done by gravity is \(400\,\mathrm J\).

glossary.definition: Energy transferred by a force through displacement.
The line along which a force acts.
The positive amount equal in magnitude to the negative work of the resistance.
One newton metre, the unit of work and energy.

examples.title: Find signed work from an angle
examples.question: The sample carriage moves \(15\,\mathrm m\) in a straight line. A constant force has magnitude \(28\,\mathrm N\) at angle \(60^\circ\) to the displacement. Find the signed work done by that force.
solution: The force component along the displacement is \(F\cos\theta=14\) newtons.
Multiply the signed component by the distance. \(W=28\times 15\times\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=210\).
The force does \(210\,\mathrm J\) of work. This is positive because the force partly helps the motion.

examples.title: Find signed work from an angle
examples.question: The sample carriage moves \(5\,\mathrm m\) in a straight line. A constant force has magnitude \(32\,\mathrm N\) at angle \(120^\circ\) to the displacement. Find the signed work done by that force.
solution: The force component along the displacement is \(F\cos\theta=-16\) newtons.
Multiply the signed component by the distance. \(W=32\times 5\times\left(- \frac{1}{2}\right)=-80\).
The force does \(-80\,\mathrm J\) of work. This is negative because the force has a component opposing motion.

examples.title: Find signed work from an angle
examples.question: The measuring cart moves \(22\,\mathrm m\) in a straight line. A constant force has magnitude \(14\,\mathrm N\) at angle \(180^\circ\) to the displacement. Find the signed work done by that force.
solution: The force component along the displacement is \(F\cos\theta=-14\) newtons.
Multiply the signed component by the distance. \(W=14\times 22\times\left(-1\right)=-308\).
The force does \(-308\,\mathrm J\) of work. This is negative because the force has a component opposing motion.

examples.title: Find signed work from an angle
examples.question: The marker tray moves \(8\,\mathrm m\) in a straight line. A constant force has magnitude \(54\,\mathrm N\) at angle \(90^\circ\) to the displacement. Find the signed work done by that force.
solution: The force component along the displacement is \(F\cos\theta=0\) newtons.
Multiply the signed component by the distance. \(W=54\times 8\times\left(0\right)=0\).
The force does \(0\,\mathrm J\) of work. This is zero because there is no displacement along the force.

examples.title: Distinguish work by and against a resistance
examples.question: A cart moves \(22\,\mathrm m\) against a constant resistance of \(8\,\mathrm N\). Find the signed work done by resistance and the energy lost to resistance.
solution: The force points opposite to the displacement, so its own work is \(-Rd\).
The product of the two magnitudes is \(176\,\mathrm J\).
Resistance does \(-176\,\mathrm J\) of work. The amount of energy transferred away from mechanical energy is \(176\,\mathrm J\).

examples.title: Distinguish work by and against a resistance
examples.question: A instrument trolley moves \(45\,\mathrm m\) against a constant resistance of \(\frac{11}{2}\,\mathrm N\). Find the work done against the resistance.
solution: The force points opposite to the displacement, so its own work is \(-Rd\).
The product of the two magnitudes is \(\frac{495}{2}\,\mathrm J\).
The work done against resistance is \(\frac{495}{2}\,\mathrm J\).

examples.title: Calculate work by weight on a slope
examples.question: A particle, modelled as a instrument sled, has mass \(14\,\mathrm{kg}\) moves \(20\,\mathrm m\) up a slope. The sine of the inclination is \(\frac{3}{5}\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Give its signed height change (upwards positive) and the work done by gravity.
solution: Only vertical displacement enters the work done by the vertical weight. The vertical change is \(12\,\mathrm m\).
Gravity acts downwards, so signed work is \(W_g=-mg\,\Delta h=-1680\) joules.
The height change is \(12\,\mathrm m\) and work done by gravity is \(-1680\,\mathrm J\).

orig_9709_m1_energy_kinetic_potential_en.description: Calculate KE, recover speed and compare GPE relative to a consistent height datum.

sections.title: How do mass and speed affect kinetic energy?
sections.label: Calculate kinetic energy
sections.intro: Kinetic energy is the energy associated with motion. It is determined by speed, so reversing the direction at the same speed leaves the kinetic energy unchanged.

blocks.html: \(K=\frac12mv^2\). Doubling the mass doubles \(K\) if speed is fixed. Doubling the speed multiplies \(K\) by four at fixed mass.
Square the speed before multiplying by half the mass.

blocks.title: Calculate kinetic energy
blocks.prompt: A particle of mass \(15\,\mathrm{kg}\) moves at \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find its kinetic energy.
blocks.hint: Substitute the speed, then square it. Do not square the mass.
blocks.solution:
Square the speed before multiplying by half the mass.

\(K=\frac12\times 15\times 4^2=120\).

The kinetic energy is \(120\,\mathrm J\).

sections.title: How can a kinetic energy change be negative?
sections.label: Compare the two energies
sections.intro: The particle can have positive kinetic energy at both endpoints yet lose kinetic energy between them.

blocks.html: \(\Delta K=\frac12m(v^2-u^2)\), final energy minus initial energy.
The expression \(\frac12m(v-u)^2\) gives neither the signed change nor, in general, its magnitude.

blocks.title: Calculate a signed kinetic energy change
blocks.prompt: A particle of mass \(12\,\mathrm{kg}\) changes its speed from \(9\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) to \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find its signed kinetic energy change.

retry.feedback: This uses only the final KE. A change is the final kinetic energy minus the initial kinetic energy.

blocks.hint: Subtract the two energies. Squaring the change in speed gives a different expression.
blocks.solution:
The initial and final kinetic energies are \(486\,\mathrm J\) and \(96\,\mathrm J\), respectively.

Change means final minus initial. The signed kinetic energy change is \(-390\,\mathrm J\).

sections.title: How do I find speed from a known kinetic energy?
sections.label: Find the non-negative speed
sections.intro: Undo the kinetic energy formula by isolating the speed squared. Speed is a magnitude, so take the non-negative square root.

blocks.html: \(v=\sqrt{\frac{2K}{m}}\) when the mass is positive.
A negative velocity may describe direction on a chosen axis. A negative speed is impossible.

blocks.title: Recover speed from kinetic energy
blocks.prompt: A trolley has mass \(9\,\mathrm{kg}\) and kinetic energy \(225\,\mathrm J\). Find its exact speed.
blocks.hint: First multiply the kinetic energy by two and divide by mass, then take the non-negative square root.
blocks.solution:
Isolate the square of speed. \(v^2=\frac{2K}{m}=50\).

Speed is non-negative. Its exact value is \(5 \sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

sections.title: Why does the reference level matter for GPE?
sections.label: Compare heights from a common level
sections.intro: Choose a height that is convenient to call zero. The GPE relative to that level may be negative, while the difference between two GPE values is the same for every choice of reference.

blocks.html: \(U=mgh\) for a chosen height origin, and \(\Delta U=mg(h_2-h_1)\).

figure.alt: A dashed datum line lies between a higher point B and a lower point A. Vertical dashed projections mark their signed heights.
figure.caption: Use one datum for both points. The lower point has a negative height relative to this datum, but the change from A to B is positive.

blocks.html: Use the same reference before and after. A descent lowers GPE even when both heights are positive.

blocks.title: Calculate the potential energy change
blocks.prompt: A particle of mass \(6\,\mathrm{kg}\) moves from height \(-3\,\mathrm m\) to height \(2\,\mathrm m\) relative to the same reference level. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Calculate its signed gravitational potential energy change.

fields.label: Gravitational potential energy change in joules

retry.feedback: The final point is above the datum and the initial point below it. The particle has gained height and GPE.

blocks.hint: Use final height minus starting height. A descent gives a negative change in potential energy.
blocks.solution:
The height change is final minus initial: \(\Delta h=5\).

The signed gravitational potential energy change is \(\Delta U=mg\,\Delta h=300\) joules.

sections.title: What makes up mechanical energy in this model?
sections.label: Add KE and GPE
sections.intro: At each position, compute kinetic energy from its speed and GPE from its height. Their sum is the mechanical energy relative to the chosen reference.

blocks.html: Use \(E=K+U=\frac12mv^2+mgh\). The mechanical energy can change when external work is done or energy is dissipated.
An object at rest may still have non-zero GPE relative to the chosen level.
Label separate values \(K\), \(U\) and \(E\) rather than using ‘energy’ for all three.

blocks.title: Combine kinetic and potential energy
blocks.prompt: A particle of mass \(8\,\mathrm{kg}\) moves at \(7\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) at height \(-4\,\mathrm m\) relative to a stated reference level. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find its kinetic energy, gravitational potential energy and total mechanical energy relative to this level.
blocks.hint: Use the reference height given in the question. A negative height gives negative GPE, while kinetic energy cannot be negative.
blocks.solution:
Kinetic energy is \(K=\frac12mv^2=196\) joules.

Gravitational potential energy relative to the reference is \(U=mgh=-320\) joules.

The kinetic and potential energies are \(196\,\mathrm J\) and \(-320\,\mathrm J\), so the total mechanical energy is \(-124\,\mathrm J\).

glossary.definition: Energy associated with the speed of a moving particle.
Energy relative to a chosen height reference in a uniform gravitational field.
The sum of kinetic and gravitational potential energy in this model.

examples.title: Calculate kinetic energy
examples.question: A particle of mass \(6\,\mathrm{kg}\) moves at \(9\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find its kinetic energy.
solution: Square the speed before multiplying by half the mass.
\(K=\frac12\times 6\times 9^2=243\).
The kinetic energy is \(243\,\mathrm J\).

solution: The initial and final kinetic energies are \(\frac{605}{2}\,\mathrm J\) and \(\frac{245}{2}\,\mathrm J\), respectively.
Change means final minus initial. The signed kinetic energy change is \(-180\,\mathrm J\).

solution: The initial and final kinetic energies are \(\frac{441}{2}\,\mathrm J\) and \(648\,\mathrm J\), respectively.

examples.title: Recover speed from kinetic energy
examples.question: A trolley has mass \(8\,\mathrm{kg}\) and kinetic energy \(100\,\mathrm J\). Find its exact speed.
solution: Isolate the square of speed. \(v^2=\frac{2K}{m}=25\).
Speed is non-negative. Its exact value is \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

examples.title: Recover speed from kinetic energy
examples.question: A trolley has mass \(12\,\mathrm{kg}\) and kinetic energy \(486\,\mathrm J\). Find its exact speed.
solution: Isolate the square of speed. \(v^2=\frac{2K}{m}=81\).
Speed is non-negative. Its exact value is \(9\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

examples.title: Calculate the potential energy change
examples.question: A particle of mass \(12\,\mathrm{kg}\) moves from height \(8\,\mathrm m\) to height \(3\,\mathrm m\) relative to the same reference level. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Calculate its signed gravitational potential energy change.
solution: The height change is final minus initial: \(\Delta h=-5\).
The signed gravitational potential energy change is \(\Delta U=mg\,\Delta h=-600\) joules.

examples.title: Combine kinetic and potential energy
examples.question: A particle of mass \(5\,\mathrm{kg}\) moves at \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) at height \(3\,\mathrm m\) relative to a stated reference level. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find its kinetic energy, gravitational potential energy and total mechanical energy relative to this level.
solution: Kinetic energy is \(K=\frac12mv^2=40\) joules.
Gravitational potential energy relative to the reference is \(U=mgh=150\) joules.
The kinetic and potential energies are \(40\,\mathrm J\) and \(150\,\mathrm J\), so the total mechanical energy is \(190\,\mathrm J\).

revision.body:
Choose the method

UseWhat to write
Kinetic energy\(K=\frac12mv^2\), using speed \(v\ge0\).
Change in KE\(\Delta K=\frac12m(v^2-u^2)\).
Potential energy\(U=mgh\) relative to the chosen datum.
Change in GPE\(\Delta U=mg(h_f-h_i)\).
Mechanical energy\(E=K+U\).
revision.checks:
• Square speed before multiplying.
  • Use final minus initial for a change.
  • Keep the same height datum for both states.
revision.examTip: If a question asks for energy relative to a datum, keep the sign. Energy changes are independent of datum.

orig_9709_m1_energy_energy_principle.description: Balance KE, GPE, work by a driving force and dissipation at endpoints of smooth or rough motion.

sections.title: What belongs on each side of an energy equation?
sections.label: Write one signed balance
sections.intro: Decide which body or combination of bodies is the system. Include gravity through a signed GPE change, then include driving work and resistive loss separately.

blocks.html: With positive loss \(L\), use \(K_f+\Delta U=K_i+W_{\rm drive}-L\). This is equivalent to \(\Delta K\) equalling the net work when gravity is written as work instead.
Do not include gravity as work and also include it as GPE change in the same equation.

blocks.title: Find a speed using an energy balance
blocks.prompt: A trial pod of mass \(10\,\mathrm{kg}\) enters a track at \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). It falls by \(2\,\mathrm m\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). There is no driving force. Resistive forces dissipate \(94\,\mathrm J\). Find the exact speed at the end.

fields.label: Exact speed in metres per second

blocks.hint: Use final minus initial for GPE. Count gravity in that change and count only non-gravitational work on the other side.
blocks.solution:
Use \(K_f+\Delta U=K_i+W_{\rm drive}-L\), where \(L\) is the positive amount dissipated.

The initial kinetic energy is \(125\,\mathrm J\) and the signed potential energy change is \(-200\,\mathrm J\).

Substituting the work and the potential energy change gives \(K_f=231\) joules.

The final kinetic energy is \(231\,\mathrm J\), so the exact final speed is \(\frac{\sqrt{1155}}{5}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

sections.title: Why can height be enough on a curved track?
sections.label: Conserve mechanical energy
sections.intro: For motion on a fixed smooth surface with no drag, the normal reaction is perpendicular to the instantaneous motion. It does no work, so energy can give information about the endpoints without finding forces along the curve.

blocks.html: A vertical drop \(h\) gives \(v^2=u^2+2gh\), when there are no other energy transfers and contact continues.

figure.alt: A track descends from A to B and then rises. Dashed horizontal guides connect A and B to a vertical height marker.
figure.caption: Even on a curved track, the height difference between A and B fixes the change in GPE.

blocks.html: The energy method gives speed. It does not determine time or the changing normal reaction.

blocks.title: Find speed on a smooth curved track
blocks.prompt: A particle enters a smooth curved track at \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). It remains in contact and reaches a point \(\frac{7}{5}\,\mathrm m\) vertically below the entry. Neglect drag. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find its exact speed at this point.

fields.label: Exact speed in metres per second

blocks.hint: Use the difference in height between endpoints. The curve length and its varying slope are unnecessary.
blocks.solution:
The normal force is perpendicular to the instantaneous movement. It does no work, and no energy is dissipated.

The loss of gravitational potential energy equals the gain in kinetic energy.

sections.title: Which distance belongs with friction?
sections.label: Compute dissipated work
sections.intro: Resistance transfers energy along the full distance travelled. Gravity still depends only on the vertical displacement of the particle.

blocks.html: For constant resistance \(R\) over length \(d\), write \(L=Rd\). Enter \(mg\Delta h\) separately.
Using the slope length for the change in GPE, or the height change for friction, mixes different physical quantities.

blocks.title: Use friction distance separately from height
blocks.prompt: A sled of mass \(5\,\mathrm{kg}\) enters a straight section at \(12\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). It travels \(10\,\mathrm m\) along the section and climbs by \(3\,\mathrm m\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). A constant resistance of \(12\,\mathrm N\) opposes the movement. Find its exact exit speed.

fields.label: Exit speed in metres per second

blocks.hint: Use the path length for work by friction and the vertical change for potential energy.

The path length belongs in resistive work. The height change belongs in gravitational potential energy.

sections.title: How do I find energy lost if only μ is given?

sections.intro: For a particle sliding along a straight rough plane in this model, first obtain the normal reaction from the perpendicular forces. Then use the sliding friction magnitude and path length.

blocks.html: With weight as the only force with a perpendicular component, \(R=mg\cos\alpha\) and \(L=\mu Rd\).
If an applied force presses into the plane or lifts partly off it, the normal reaction changes.

blocks.title: Find energy loss from the sliding friction model
blocks.prompt: A particle of mass \(8\,\mathrm{kg}\) moves up a straight rough incline. Its entry speed is \(15\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and the on-slope journey is \(6\,\mathrm m\). The sine of the inclination is \(\frac{5}{13}\) and the coefficient of friction is \(\frac{1}{6}\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find the exact work done against friction and its exact speed at the end.

blocks.hint: Calculate the normal force first. The friction loss uses the full on-slope distance.
blocks.solution:
No other force has a perpendicular component, so the normal reaction is \(R=mg\cos\alpha=\frac{960}{13}\) newtons.

While sliding, the frictional force has magnitude \(\mu R=\frac{160}{13}\) newtons. Its energy loss along the slope is \(\frac{960}{13}\,\mathrm J\).

The height gain is \(\frac{30}{13}\,\mathrm m\) and GPE gain is \(\frac{2400}{13}\,\mathrm J\). The initial energy minus these two costs gives \(\frac{8340}{13}\,\mathrm J\) of final kinetic energy.

The work done against friction is \(\frac{960}{13}\,\mathrm J\) and the exact final speed is \(\frac{\sqrt{27105}}{13}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

sections.title: How can speed readings reveal a loss or driving work?
sections.label: Rearrange the balance
sections.intro: When both endpoint speeds are known, evaluate both kinetic energies. The remaining change in GPE and known work terms can then isolate the missing contribution.

blocks.html: Rearrange to find either \(L=K_i+W_{\rm drive}-\Delta U-K_f\) or \(W_{\rm drive}=\Delta K+\Delta U+L\).

blocks.title: Find the driving work
blocks.prompt: A trial pod of mass \(9\,\mathrm{kg}\) enters a track at \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). It rises by \(4\,\mathrm m\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Resistive forces dissipate \(89\,\mathrm J\). It leaves at exact speed \(\frac{\sqrt{527}}{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find the work done by the driving force.
blocks.hint: Use final minus initial for GPE. Count gravity in that change and count only non-gravitational work on the other side.
blocks.solution:
Use \(K_f+\Delta U=K_i+W_{\rm drive}-L\), where \(L\) is the positive amount dissipated.

The initial kinetic energy is \(\frac{225}{2}\,\mathrm J\) and the signed potential energy change is \(360\,\mathrm J\).

The final kinetic energy is \(\frac{527}{2}\,\mathrm J\). Thus driving work is the kinetic energy change plus the GPE change plus dissipated energy.

The driving force does \(600\,\mathrm J\) of work.

examples.title: Infer the dissipated energy

sections.title: When should I split a journey into stages?
sections.label: Mark each change of conditions
sections.intro: Split the route at boundaries where a different force acts, the resistance changes or an intermediate speed is requested. A stage can otherwise be treated as one energy balance.

blocks.html: At a boundary without an impact or stated loss, the last kinetic energy of the earlier stage becomes the first of the next stage.

figure.alt: The cart route drops from A to B, then continues along a level section from B to C. B is marked as a stage boundary.
figure.caption: Use separate work and energy equations for AB and BC. The energy at B connects them.

blocks.html: Do not reuse the original speed at a later boundary. Calculate the boundary speed or carry its kinetic energy forwards.

blocks.title: Carry kinetic energy between two stages
blocks.prompt: A rail cart of mass \(8\,\mathrm{kg}\) moves from \(A\) at \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Straight section \(AB\) is \(13\,\mathrm m\) long and drops vertically by \(4\,\mathrm m\). Its constant resistance is \(10\,\mathrm N\). The following level stretch \(BC\) is \(22\,\mathrm m\) long, with no energy lost at the transition. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Its constant resistance on \(BC\) is \(4\,\mathrm N\). Find the exact speeds at \(B\) and \(C\).

fields.label: Speed at B in metres per second
Speed at C in metres per second

blocks.hint: Use the final kinetic energy of AB as the initial kinetic energy of BC. Use each section’s own resistance and length.
blocks.solution:
For \(AB\), gravity releases \(320\,\mathrm J\) and resistance dissipates \(130\,\mathrm J\).

The kinetic energy at \(B\) is \(K_B=16+320-130=206\) joules, giving speed \(\frac{\sqrt{206}}{2}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

On \(BC\), there is no GPE change. The energy loss is \(88\,\mathrm J\), leaving \(118\,\mathrm J\).

The speeds are \(\frac{\sqrt{206}}{2}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) at \(B\) and \(\frac{\sqrt{118}}{2}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) at \(C\).

sections.title: How can I recover a resistance on a later section?
sections.label: Use stage-specific losses
sections.intro: Calculate the kinetic energy entering the later section. Use the known final speed to calculate the remaining kinetic energy. The difference tells you what was transferred out on that section, after accounting for any work or height change.

blocks.html: On a level unpowered section with constant resistance, \(R=\frac{K_{\rm entry}-K_{\rm exit}}{d}\).
Do not divide a total-route loss by the distance of just one stage.

blocks.title: Carry kinetic energy between two stages
blocks.prompt: A rail cart of mass \(7\,\mathrm{kg}\) moves from \(A\) at \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Straight section \(AB\) is \(10\,\mathrm m\) long and drops vertically by \(2\,\mathrm m\). Its constant resistance is \(9\,\mathrm N\). The following level stretch \(BC\) is \(9\,\mathrm m\) long, with no energy lost at the transition. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). The cart leaves \(C\) at exact speed \(\frac{\sqrt{574}}{7}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find its exact speed at \(B\) and the constant resistance on \(BC\).

fields.label: Speed at B in metres per second

blocks.hint: Use the final kinetic energy of AB as the initial kinetic energy of BC. Use each section’s own resistance and length.
blocks.solution:
For \(AB\), gravity releases \(140\,\mathrm J\) and resistance dissipates \(90\,\mathrm J\).

The kinetic energy at \(B\) is \(K_B=126+140-90=176\) joules, giving speed \(\frac{4 \sqrt{154}}{7}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

On \(BC\), there is no GPE change. The given final speed gives \(41\,\mathrm J\) of kinetic energy.

The speed at \(B\) is \(\frac{4 \sqrt{154}}{7}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), and the resistance on \(BC\) is \(R_2=\frac{K_B-K_C}{d_2}=15\) newtons.

sections.title: How far does the particle travel after reaching a new surface?
sections.label: Use zero energy at the stop
sections.intro: The motion may continue after leaving a slope. Find the kinetic energy at the bottom, then use the new resistance to determine the distance before the first stop.

blocks.html: On a level run with constant resistance, \(d=\frac{K_{\rm entry}}R\) until speed reaches zero.
That stopping distance is measured from the start of the run. Add the earlier slope length only if total route length is requested.

blocks.title: Find the level stopping distance after a descent
blocks.prompt: A sled of mass \(10\,\mathrm{kg}\) enters a straight slope at \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The slope length is \(12\,\mathrm m\), with vertical drop \(3\,\mathrm m\) and constant resistance \(15\,\mathrm N\). It then travels onto a level run with constant resistance \(20\,\mathrm N\), retaining its speed as it enters the run. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). How far does it travel on the level run before first coming to rest?

retry.feedback: This accounts for the entry KE only. Carry the extra energy gained on the descent into the level stage with its own resistance.

blocks.hint: Find the intermediate energy at the slope foot, then use zero final speed on the level section.
blocks.solution:
Find the energy at the foot of the incline. It is the initial kinetic energy plus gravitational energy released, minus the work against the first resistance.

This leaves \(K_B=80+300-180=200\) joules.

On the level part the height is constant. The resistance does work against the remaining kinetic energy until the sled stops.

\(d=\frac{K_B}{R_2}=10\). The level stopping distance is \(10\,\mathrm m\).

sections.title: Can resistance do negative work in both directions?
sections.label: Track the outward and return distances
sections.intro: If a particle reverses direction, friction reverses too. Friction opposes the movement on both legs and transfers mechanical energy away on each one.

blocks.html: For a round trip over the same distance \(d\) each way with constant resistance magnitude, the loss is \(2Rd\). The final GPE relative to the start is unchanged.
Zero overall displacement does not imply zero resistive work. Each leg has its own displacement and resistance direction.

blocks.title: Account for resistance on both legs
blocks.prompt: A particle of mass \(8\,\mathrm{kg}\) is projected up a rough slope at \(7\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and reaches its turning point after \(4\,\mathrm m\). The sine of the inclination is \(\frac{1}{2}\). The same constant resistance acts opposite to the motion on the outward and return journeys. The particle begins to slide back down at the turning point. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find the resistance and the exact speed at which it returns to the starting point.

fields.label: Return speed in metres per second

blocks.hint: The two friction forces have opposite directions, but each does negative work because the motion direction also reverses.
blocks.solution:
At the turning point the speed is zero. The height gain is \(2\,\mathrm m\), so the outward energy balance is \(196=160+4R\).

This gives a resistance of \(9\,\mathrm N\). Between start and return, height is unchanged but resistance transfers energy away on both legs.

The remaining kinetic energy is \(124\,\mathrm J\). The resistance is \(9\,\mathrm N\) and the exact return speed is \(\sqrt{31}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

sections.title: How do I balance energy for two connected particles?
sections.label: Include both particles
sections.intro: When a light taut string runs over a smooth pulley, its tension does positive work on one particle and equal negative work on the other for equal displacements. Its net contribution cancels if both particles are included in the system.

blocks.html: Add both kinetic energies and both signed GPE changes. A rise and fall of equal length do not imply equal energy changes if the masses differ.

figure.alt: Two particles A and B hang from a light string over a pulley. A moves up and B moves down.
figure.caption: The equal distances occur in opposite directions. Tension adds energy to the rising particle and removes the same amount from the descending particle.

blocks.html: Do not cancel the tension work if analysing just one particle.

blocks.title: Choose both connected particles as the system
blocks.prompt: Particles of masses \(4\,\mathrm{kg}\) and \(6\,\mathrm{kg}\) hang at the ends of a light inextensible string over a smooth pulley. The string remains taut. The lighter particle rises \(\frac{5}{2}\,\mathrm m\) while the heavier particle descends the same distance. Their common initial speed is \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Ignore air resistance. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find the system's signed GPE change and the exact final common speed.

fields.label: Exact common speed in metres per second

blocks.hint: Track a rise and a fall of the same distance. Use both masses in KE, and the difference of their signed GPE changes.
blocks.solution:
The light string pulls both particles with equal tension. Its work on the ascending particle is positive and the same magnitude as its negative work on the descending particle.

The signed change of GPE is \(\Delta U=(m_{\rm up}-m_{\rm down})gd=-50\) joules.

Both particles have the same speed. Use the combined mass \(10\,\mathrm{kg}\) to find the change in total kinetic energy.

The system gains \(50\,\mathrm J\) of kinetic energy. Its GPE change is \(-50\,\mathrm J\) and the exact final speed is \(\sqrt{19}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

examples.title: Find the level stopping distance after a descent
examples.question: A sled of mass \(5\,\mathrm{kg}\) enters a straight slope at \(7\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The slope length is \(9\,\mathrm m\), with vertical drop \(2\,\mathrm m\) and constant resistance \(11\,\mathrm N\). It then travels onto a level run with constant resistance \(24\,\mathrm N\), retaining its speed as it enters the run. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). How far does it travel on the level run before first coming to rest?
solution: Find the energy at the foot of the incline. It is the initial kinetic energy plus gravitational energy released, minus the work against the first resistance.
This leaves \(K_B=\frac{245}{2}+100-99=\frac{247}{2}\) joules.
On the level part the height is constant. The resistance does work against the remaining kinetic energy until the sled stops.
\(d=\frac{K_B}{R_2}=\frac{247}{48}\). The level stopping distance is \(\frac{247}{48}\,\mathrm m\).

examples.title: Account for resistance on both legs
examples.question: A particle of mass \(5\,\mathrm{kg}\) is projected up a rough slope at \(8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and reaches its turning point after \(4\,\mathrm m\). The sine of the inclination is \(\frac{3}{5}\). The same constant resistance acts opposite to the motion on the outward and return journeys. The particle begins to slide back down at the turning point. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find the resistance and the exact speed at which it returns to the starting point.
solution: At the turning point the speed is zero. The height gain is \(\frac{12}{5}\,\mathrm m\), so the outward energy balance is \(160=120+4R\).
This gives a resistance of \(10\,\mathrm N\). Between start and return, height is unchanged but resistance transfers energy away on both legs.
The remaining kinetic energy is \(80\,\mathrm J\). The resistance is \(10\,\mathrm N\) and the exact return speed is \(4 \sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

examples.title: Choose both connected particles as the system
examples.question: Particles of masses \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) and \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\) hang at the ends of a light inextensible string over a smooth pulley. The string remains taut. The lighter particle rises \(2\,\mathrm m\) while the heavier particle descends the same distance. Their common initial speed is \(1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Ignore air resistance. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find the system's signed GPE change and the exact final common speed.
solution: The light string pulls both particles with equal tension. Its work on the ascending particle is positive and the same magnitude as its negative work on the descending particle.
The signed change of GPE is \(\Delta U=(m_{\rm up}-m_{\rm down})gd=-20\) joules.
Both particles have the same speed. Use the combined mass \(5\,\mathrm{kg}\) to find the change in total kinetic energy.
The system gains \(20\,\mathrm J\) of kinetic energy. Its GPE change is \(-20\,\mathrm J\) and the exact final speed is \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

sections.title: What is the difference between work and power?
sections.label: Find an average rate
sections.intro: Work is an amount of energy transferred. Power states how fast that work is done. A fixed amount of work completed sooner has a greater average power.

blocks.html: \(P_{\rm avg}=\frac{W}{t}\). A watt is a joule per second and \(1\,\mathrm{kW}=1000\,\mathrm W\).
Convert minutes to seconds first. Do not divide energy in joules by time in minutes and label the result as watts.

blocks.title: Use work and elapsed time
blocks.prompt: A motor does \(45\,\mathrm{kJ}\) of work in \(15\,\mathrm{s}\). Find its average power in kilowatts.
blocks.hint: Convert to consistent units before dividing. A kilowatt is a thousand watts and a minute is sixty seconds.
blocks.solution:
Convert to joules and seconds: \(45000\,\mathrm J\) in \(15\,\mathrm s\). Divide work by time.

Use \(P_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{W}{t}\). This relates an entire interval to one average value.

The average power is \(3\,\mathrm{kW}\).

sections.title: Which force belongs in P = Fv?
sections.label: Use the driving force at that instant
sections.intro: If a force acts along the motion, its instantaneous power is the force magnitude times the speed. The engine’s power therefore gives the engine force at a known speed.

blocks.html: For forward driving, \(P=Fv\). Use \(F=\frac Pv\) when \(v>0\). At fixed power a faster vehicle has a smaller driving force.
The engine force differs from the resultant force whenever there is resistance or a component of weight along the road.

blocks.title: Link engine power and the driving force
blocks.prompt: A carrier moves at \(12\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) at a given instant. Its engine develops \(\frac{27}{5}\,\mathrm{kW}\). The driving force acts in the direction of motion. Find its magnitude.
blocks.hint: Use the force exerted by the engine and the speed at that instant. Resistance is not the driving force.
blocks.solution:
Convert the engine output to \(5400\,\mathrm W\).

Use \(F=\frac{P}{v}=450\). The driving force is \(450\,\mathrm N\).

sections.title: How do resistance and slope affect steady speed?
sections.label: Balance forces before using power
sections.intro: At steady speed the resultant along the road is zero. Uphill, the engine balances resistance and the slope component of weight. Downhill, gravity assists the engine against resistance.

blocks.html: With positive direction along motion, use \(F=R+mg\sin\alpha\) uphill and \(F=R-mg\sin\alpha\) downhill when the engine still drives forward.
The same power need not produce the same steady speed on a hill and a level road.

blocks.title: Find steady speed or instantaneous acceleration
blocks.prompt: A small vehicle of mass \(800\,\mathrm{kg}\) moves straight downhill along a road whose sine of inclination is \(\frac{1}{25}\). A constant resistance of \(800\,\mathrm N\) acts against the motion. The engine supplies \(\frac{48}{5}\,\mathrm{kW}\) in the direction of motion. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find the steady speed when this power is maintained.

fields.label: Steady speed in metres per second

retry.feedback: This divides by resistance only. Downhill, gravity supplies part of the force needed for steady speed.

blocks.hint: Calculate the driving force from power first if speed is known. Keep the weight component, resistance and driving force separate.
blocks.solution:
At steady speed the force resultant along the road is zero. Weight contributes a signed opposition of \(-320\,\mathrm N\) and resistance contributes \(800\,\mathrm N\).

Balance forces to give engine driving force \(480\,\mathrm N\).

Use \(v=\frac{P}{F}=20\). The steady speed is \(20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

sections.title: What if the vehicle is speeding up or slowing down?
sections.label: Find the force resultant at the instant
sections.intro: Use the actual speed at the specified instant to obtain the driving force. Then use the signed force equation along the road. The result can be negative even when the vehicle is moving forwards.

blocks.html: Along the motion, \(ma=F-R-mg\sin\alpha\) uphill. Determine \(F\) from \(P\) and \(v\) before substituting.

figure.alt: A vehicle on a slope has driving force uphill, resistance downhill and weight vertically down. Motion is uphill.
figure.caption: Use the driving force in the power equation. Resolve weight and resistance separately for the net uphill force.

blocks.html: Setting the resultant to zero assumes steady speed. That assumption is invalid when acceleration is requested.

blocks.title: Find steady speed or instantaneous acceleration
blocks.prompt: A small vehicle of mass \(780\,\mathrm{kg}\) moves straight uphill along a road whose sine of inclination is \(\frac{1}{13}\). A constant resistance of \(280\,\mathrm N\) acts against the motion. The engine supplies \(\frac{352}{25}\,\mathrm{kW}\) in the direction of motion. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find the driving force and the signed acceleration at the instant its speed is \(20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The direction of motion is positive.

fields.label: Signed acceleration in metres per second squared

blocks.hint: Calculate the driving force from power first if speed is known. Keep the weight component, resistance and driving force separate.
blocks.solution:
Find the driving force from \(F=\frac{P}{v}=704\) newtons.

The opposition to forward motion is \(280\,\mathrm N\) from resistance plus \(600\,\mathrm N\) as the signed weight contribution.

Newton’s second law along the motion gives \(ma=704-\left(880\right)\).

The driving force is \(704\,\mathrm N\) and signed acceleration is \(- \frac{44}{195}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

sections.title: Where does the engine's work go at steady speed?
sections.label: Compare energy transfer rates
sections.intro: At steady speed the rate of gain of kinetic energy is zero. The engine may still be raising the height and replacing energy dissipated by resistance.

blocks.html: Uphill at speed \(v\), GPE increases at rate \(mgv\sin\alpha\) and resistive loss is \(Rv\).
Zero acceleration does not imply zero engine power. It says that the kinetic energy stays constant.
As a check, engine power should equal the total opposing force multiplied by the speed when the speed is steady.

A constant resistance of \(600\,\mathrm N\) acts against motion. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find the rate of gain of GPE, the rate of energy dissipation through resistance, and the engine power, all in watts.

blocks.hint: At steady speed the engine must supply both the potential energy gain and the energy dissipated against resistance.
blocks.solution:
The vertical speed is \(\frac{3}{4}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), so GPE increases by \(6000\,\mathrm W\) as a rate.

The resistive force dissipates \(9000\,\mathrm W\). Steady speed means there is no rate of gain of kinetic energy.

The GPE gain rate is \(6000\,\mathrm W\), the dissipation rate is \(9000\,\mathrm W\), and the engine power is \(15000\,\mathrm W\).
